 Why Food Safety Culture Must Include Recall Readiness
 Nov 
 18 
 2026 
 Feature
 Adobe Stock 
 Ineffective recalls can have serious, long-term, and costly consequences, including increasing public health risks and eroding consumer trust. 
 Share: Tweet Facebook LinkedIn Email 
 Recall readiness must be an output of food safety culture. 
 Food safety culture is one of the industry’s most talked-about priorities, especially in the wake of the recent, large-scale food recalls, including lettuce , jalapeños , meat , eggs , and blueberries . Many restaurant brands have invested heavily in developing strong food safety cultures, with training and education at the forefront of these efforts. At the same time, the recent string of widespread food recalls spotlights something those programs don’t always address: whether the culture extends to recall preparation. After all, your restaurant doesn’t truly have a good food safety culture if you aren’t recall ready.
 Recall readiness is food safety culture tested under pressure . Consider this: if your restaurant received contaminated lettuce, tainted meat, or other products involved in a recall, would your team know exactly what to do? Even if you have an exceptional food safety culture “on paper,” would this culture drive proper behaviors and decisions in practice, as employees are under extreme pressure?
 A Recall Gap Puts Guests at Risk 
 Food safety culture with a gap at the recall level isn’t actually a strong food safety culture. Likewise, recall readiness doesn’t hold up without the cultural infrastructure supporting it. Neither initiative stands alone. 
 Think seriously about whether your food safety culture extends to recall readiness. In many companies, recall preparation gets postponed due to its low-frequency nature, with brands earmarking their budgets and resources to daily food safety culture work instead. Unfortunately, recall readiness is a vital part of the culture, at the corporate level down to locations—yet it’s frequently put off until it’s too late.
 A strong food safety culture requires alignment between your company’s daily food safety protocols and your emergency response protocols. A breakdown during a recall is a systemic failure that can put your consumers, trading partners, and brand at risk.
 A Recall Gap Undermines Food Safety Culture 
 When a food recall occurs, your company needs a proper, coordinated, and organized response to protect public health, your supply chain, and your brand reputation. Restaurant company leaders must ask themselves:
 What’s the extent of your food safety culture? Passing safety audits or hanging a certification in your restaurant locations is important, but these things don’t necessarily translate to a safe culture. Sometimes, food businesses mistake this documentation for “proof” of an outstanding food safety culture. Similarly, if a location runs through their checklists—they’ve completed food safety training, they passed a third-party audit, their teams regularly perform safety checks, etc.—they believe they have tangible evidence of an A+ food safety culture. However, food safety culture is actually tested when your team is under extreme pressure during a recall situation. If you’re truly recall ready, your team will be well-prepared and equipped to manage the situation properly: containing the recall, minimizing damages, and protecting public health. If you’re not recall ready, the opposite will be true. Being unprepared to handle a recall puts you and your trading partners at risk for major financial, legal, operational, and reputational damage. Remember: the gap between what your employees are supposed to do and what they actually do can make your guests, business, and trading partners vulnerable in a recall.  
 What’s your commitment to recall readiness? Food safety culture and recall readiness starts at the top. Do you prioritize both food safety culture and recall preparedness? Do you explain why this matters to help secure employee buy-in? Did you train your team, define accountability, assign key roles, and practice with your trading partners in advance of a recall? Mock recall simulations are especially valuable, providing hands-on practice for teams and partners, from recall initiation through resolution. Participating in these continuous improvement exercises is valuable for identifying and correcting knowledge gaps, ensuring that teams will be comfortable and confident to manage a real-world crisis. 
 Have you assembled a cross-functional team? A recall team must involve more than just the company’s CEO or operational leaders. Assemble a cross-functional team before a recall event occurs, and ensure they understand their roles and responsibilities in advance. This team must include quality, operations, IT, legal, and communications working from the same process.
 Do your employees feel empowered to flag safety issues? It’s essential to incorporate employee empowerment into your food safety culture. Emphasize your commitment to “no-blame reporting”, where frontline staff are encouraged to flag safety concerns or recall process concerns without fear of blame or repercussions. When every employee feels like a food safety ambassador, equally responsible for identifying potential food safety or recall concerns, the entire company and its guests benefit.
 Are you prepared in advance of a recall? The recent, wide-scale recalls have demonstrated that data management is more important than ever before. Therefore, prioritize transparency and documentation, ensuring that you have current contact data, traceability records, and the ability to confirm that key actions—like product removal—have actually happened. Interoperable tech systems are essential for this effort, allowing you and your trading partners to improve visibility, trackability, collaboration, and info-sharing during a stressful, time-sensitive recall event—but they must be implemented before a recall happens to make a difference.
 Recall readiness must be an output of food safety culture. Don’t mistake a strong food safety culture for proof that recall preparation is covered. 
 Roger Hancock, CEO of Recall InfoLink , is one of the world’s foremost experts on recalls, with experience that spans the retail, tech, data, regulatory, and supply chain. Recall InfoLink makes recalls faster, easier, and more accurate across the supply chain to protect consumers and brands. As the only company focused entirely on recalls, Recall InfoLink’s solutions drive immediate action, streamline the recall process, and simplify compliance. Roger is also a steering committee member of the Alliance for Recall Ready Communities .
